examples.question_text: Find the coordinates of $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ on the unit circle when $\theta=145^{\circ}$. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

examples.solution_text:
$\sin255^{\circ}$ is the $y$-coordinate. The point lies below the $x$-axis, so $\sin255^{\circ}<0$.

$\cos255^{\circ}$ is the $x$-coordinate. The point lies left of the $y$-axis, so $\cos255^{\circ}<0$.

examples.question_text: State the exact coordinates of $P(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ when $\theta=0^{\circ}$ and when $\theta=360^{\circ}$. Hence state the sine and cosine of each angle.
A point on the unit circle has $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=-1$. State its coordinates and the angle $\theta$ in $0^{\circ}\le\theta<360^{\circ}$.

examples.derivation: Independently evaluated cos145° ≈ -0.819152 and sin145° ≈ 0.573576, giving P ≈ (-0.82,0.57). The radius and perpendicular place P in quadrant 2, consistent with both coordinate signs. This follows the coordinate definitions and rounding task in source lines 813–901.

255° lies strictly between 180° and 270°, placing P left of the y-axis and below the x-axis. Sine is its negative y-coordinate; cosine is its negative x-coordinate. The diagram matches this position. The explanation follows source lines 781–813 and the coordinate-sign reasoning in lines 1034–1043.

At 0°, the unit radius ends at (1,0); rotating through 360° returns to that point. Consequently cosine equals 1 and sine equals 0 at both angles. The diagram correctly shows the positive horizontal radius. Source lines 838–881 support boundary-coordinate interpretation, and lines 654–671 support the full-turn equivalence.

The supplied cosine and sine values give P=(0,-1), the bottom point of the unit circle. Its unique angle in 0°≤θ<360° is 270°. The downward radius and anticlockwise 270° arc agree. Source lines 857–868 and 1603–1605 support this boundary-point interpretation.
